text: Neanderthals were a kind of human who lived in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia from about 400,000 to about 40,000 years ago. They were close relatives of our own species, *Homo sapiens*, a bit like cousins on the family tree of [[@human-evolution|human evolution]].

They were shorter and stockier than most people today, with big noses, wide chests and very strong arms. Their brains were on average as large as ours. They hunted, made tools, used fire and lived through some of the coldest parts of the last [[@ice-ages|Ice Age]]. When modern humans spread out of Africa, the two groups met, and sometimes had children together.

sec.t:
In 1856, quarry workers digging in a cave in the Neander Valley, near Düsseldorf in Germany, found some heavy bones and a thick skull cap. At first, people thought they belonged to a sick modern man. Gradually scientists realised they were from a different kind of human, and named it after the valley.

Since then, remains of hundreds of Neanderthals have been found, from Spain and Gibraltar to Iraq and Siberia. No Neanderthal fossils have been found in India, though other early humans were living here at the same time.

A Neanderthal's short, solid body held heat well, a little like how a round snowman melts slower than a thin icicle. They lived in caves and rock shelters, wore animal skins and kept fires burning.

They were skilled hunters of deer, wild horses, bison and sometimes [[@mammoths|mammoths]], usually at close range with heavy spears. They also ate plants, nuts and mushrooms. Their front teeth are often heavily worn, which suggests they used their mouths like a third hand, gripping hides or tools while they worked. On the coast of Portugal, they gathered mussels and crabs. Their [[@stone-tools|stone tools]] were carefully shaped, and some were glued to wooden handles with tar made by heating birch bark, a tricky process.

In 2010, a team led by the Swedish scientist Svante Pääbo read most of the Neanderthal genome from ancient bones. Comparing it with modern [[@dna|DNA]] revealed a surprise. People whose ancestors lived outside Africa carry around 1 to 2 per cent Neanderthal DNA. Some of those genes affect skin, hair and the immune system. Pääbo won a Nobel Prize in 2022 for this work.

By about 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals had disappeared. Nobody is sure why. They may have lost out to modern humans competing for the same food. Wild swings in climate may have made life harder. Their groups were small and scattered, so bad years hit hard. And some may simply have joined modern human groups, which is how their DNA reached us.

Most likely it was a mix of all these. In a sense, Neanderthals never completely vanished. Small pieces of them are still walking around in billions of people today.

text: The oldest pieces of Earth ever found come from the Jack Hills in Western Australia. They are tiny crystals of a mineral called zircon, and some are about 4.4 billion years old. That is only about 150 million years after Earth formed.
The zircons sit inside a much younger rock. They are survivors: the rock they first grew in was worn away long ago, and they were washed into new sand and gravel.

The oldest whole rock that most geologists accept is the Acasta Gneiss (say "nice") in the far north of Canada, at about 4 billion years old. A rock belt in Quebec, also in Canada, may be older still, but scientists are still arguing about it.

st.reveal: Moving plates drag old crust down into the hot mantle, and wind, water and ice wear away what stays on top. Only a few scraps of very ancient crust have escaped all of that. Older rocks from space, called meteorites, help fill the gap.

Tall, jagged mountains are usually young, because they haven't worn down yet. The oldest rocks are mostly found in low, flat, worn-down regions called shields, such as northern Canada, Western Australia and parts of southern and eastern India.

sec.h: Why so little old rock survives
sec.t:
Earth is very good at destroying its own past. Moving plates push old ocean floor down into the hot [[mantle|mantle]], where it melts. Mountains rise and are ground down by rain, rivers and ice. Rocks get squeezed and heated until they [[@rocks-types|change into new kinds of rock]].

What survives sits in the stable, ancient hearts of continents, called cratons or shields. These are usually flat and low, worn down over billions of years. Canada, Greenland, Western Australia, southern Africa and India all have them.

sec.h: The rock nobody can agree on
sec.t:
On the eastern shore of Hudson Bay, in Quebec, lies a strip of rock called the Nuvvuagittuq belt. In 2008, a team of scientists reported that some of it might be about 4.28 billion years old. That would make it the oldest rock on Earth by a long way.

Other scientists tested the same rocks with a different chemical clock and got about 3.8 billion years. Both groups are careful researchers. The argument is about which clock gives the true age of the rock, and which only records an older ingredient that went into it. Until that is settled, Acasta keeps the title.

India has some very old rock too. The Singhbhum region, spread across Jharkhand and Odisha, and the Dharwar region of [[@karnataka|Karnataka]] both hold rocks more than 3 billion years old. Geologists study them to learn how [[@earth-layers-crust|India's piece of crust]] first formed, long before it joined and left the supercontinents of the past.

Some rocks are older than anything found on Earth, but they didn't start here. [[@meteorites|Meteorites]] are bits of asteroid that fall from the sky. Many formed about 4.56 billion years ago, as the solar system was being built, and have hardly changed since. Measuring them is one of the main ways scientists worked out the [[@earth-age|age of the Earth]].

Moon rocks help too. The Moon has no moving plates and no rain, so its surface keeps old rock better than Earth does. Some crystals in rocks brought back by the [[@moon-landing-sites|Apollo astronauts]] are about 4.4 billion years old, close to the time the [[@moon-formed|Moon formed]] after a giant collision with the young Earth.

text: GPS, the Global Positioning System, is a set of about 31 satellites circling Earth about 20,200 km up. Each one carries extremely accurate atomic clocks. It constantly broadcasts a radio message saying, in effect, "I am this satellite, I am here, and the time is now exactly this."

Your phone listens for these messages. [[@radio-waves|Radio waves]] travel at the speed of light, so by comparing when each message was sent with when it arrived, the phone works out how far away each satellite is. With distances to at least four satellites, it can calculate where on Earth it must be, often to within a few metres.

st.prompt: What is the smallest number of satellites your phone needs to work out where you are?
st.reveal: Three satellites are enough to pin down a spot in space, if your clock is perfect. Your phone's clock isn't, so it uses a fourth satellite to work out its own clock error. More satellites make the answer more accurate.

d.try: Hide a small toy in the playground or a big room. Three friends stand in different spots and each measures, with a long string or by counting steps, how far they are from the toy. Then everyone else has to find it using only those three distances. That is how GPS works.
myth: GPS satellites track your phone and know where you are.

GPS only goes one way. The satellites send out signals, and your phone listens and does the maths itself. The satellites have no idea who is listening. Apps on the phone may share your location, but that is through the internet, not GPS.

sec.t:
The trick is called trilateration. Suppose you know you are exactly 10 km from Satellite A. You could be anywhere on a giant sphere around it. Add a second satellite, and the two spheres overlap along a circle. A third narrows it to two points, and one is usually far out in space, so you know which is right.

Your phone's clock is cheap compared with a satellite's atomic clock. Light travels about 30 cm in one billionth of a second, so a tiny clock error makes a big distance error. A fourth satellite lets the phone correct its clock. Most of the time your phone can hear eight or more, which makes the answer even better.

sec.h: From military secret to everyone's phone
sec.t:
The United States [[@military|military]] began building GPS in the 1970s, launching the first satellite in 1978. It was meant for guiding troops, ships and planes. In 1983, a Korean passenger plane strayed off course into Soviet airspace and was shot down. Afterwards, the US announced that GPS would be made available for civilian use once it was ready.

At first, the signal for civilians was deliberately made less accurate. In May 2000, the US switched that off, and accuracy improved from about 100 m to about 10 m almost overnight. Car navigation, ride-hailing apps and [[@maps-digital|maps on phones]] took off.

Other countries have built their own systems so they don't depend on one country. Russia has GLONASS, Europe has Galileo and China has BeiDou. India has NavIC, Navigation with Indian Constellation, designed to use seven satellites. By mid-2026, failures had left only three of them working, so NavIC could still send time signals but could not work out positions on its own until new satellites are launched.

NavIC covers India and the region up to about 1,500 km around it. Three of its satellites are geostationary, sitting over the same spot all the time, and the others loop north and south over India. Many newer phones sold in India can use NavIC signals as well as GPS. Fishing boats have used it to find their way and receive warnings about storms.

GPS does much more than help you find your way. Its time signals keep [[@mobile-networks|mobile networks]], banks and power grids in step. Farmers use it to steer tractors in straight lines. Scientists use it to measure how much the ground moves before and after [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]], down to millimetres.

When you see a blue dot on a map, your phone has quietly done a [[@speed-distance|distance and speed]] calculation against clocks in space, using [[@coordinates|latitude and longitude]] to show the answer.

text: Sometimes, a little. Clouds are made of billions of tiny water droplets, too small and light to fall. For rain to form, droplets must grow, either by freezing into ice crystals or by bumping together into bigger drops. Each droplet or crystal needs a speck to form around, like dust or salt.

Cloud seeding adds extra specks. Planes, rockets or ground machines release tiny particles, often silver iodide or salt, into suitable clouds. If conditions are right, the cloud may drop more rain or snow than it would have. But seeding can't make clouds, and it's hard to measure how much extra rain it really brings. Scientists usually estimate somewhere between none and about 20%.

st.reveal: Clouds often have plenty of water droplets that are too small to fall. Seeding adds tiny particles, like silver iodide or salt, that help droplets freeze into ice or join together. Bigger drops and ice crystals can then fall as rain or snow.

sec.t:
This is the tricky part. You can't run the same cloud twice, once with seeding and once without. So scientists compare many seeded and unseeded clouds and use statistics.

In India, the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology ran a big experiment called CAIPEEX over Solapur, in a dry part of Maharashtra, in 2018 and 2019. Planes seeded selected monsoon clouds. Researchers reported that seeded clouds gave up to about 18% more rain, but only from the right kind of clouds, and not enough to solve a [[@droughts|drought]] alone.

In late October 2025, IIT Kanpur and the Delhi government tried cloud seeding over parts of Delhi, partly hoping rain would wash [[@air-pollution|polluted air]] clean. Planes released seeding flares, but the clouds had very little moisture. Only a trace fell, about 0.1 to 0.2 mm at a couple of spots near Delhi, too little for official weather stations to record.

Scientists said this showed a basic rule. Seeding needs moist clouds. In Delhi's dry winter season, those are rare, and polluted air usually comes back within days after rain anyway.

More than 50 countries have tried cloud seeding. China runs one of the largest programmes. The United Arab Emirates seeds clouds often to boost scarce rain. In the western USA, seeding is used over mountains to add to winter snow, which melts into rivers in spring.

Some airports and ski resorts have used it to reduce fog or boost snow. Some people worry about the silver iodide, but scientists have found the amounts used are very small. A bigger worry is fairness: if one region squeezes rain from a cloud, does a neighbour get less? So far, studies haven't shown this, but the question keeps coming up.

Weather is still far too big to control. One ordinary thunderstorm holds more energy than many atomic bombs. India's farmers will keep depending on the real [[@monsoon|monsoon]], not rain made to order.

text: For thousands of years, cattle have been at the heart of village life in India. Cows give milk, which becomes curd, [[@butter-ghee|ghee]] and paneer. Bullocks pull ploughs and carts. Dung is dried for cooking fuel, spread on fields as manure and used to plaster mud floors.

Cattle also matter for religious and cultural reasons. Many Hindus regard the cow as sacred, a gentle, giving animal linked to the god [[@myths-krishna-childhood|Krishna]], who grew up as a cowherd. Other communities in India have their own traditions and views about cattle.
Today India has about 19 crore cattle, one of the biggest herds in the world, and together with buffaloes they make it the world's biggest milk producer.

sec.t:
Indian cattle look different from the cows in a European or American picture book. They are zebu, with a hump of muscle and fat over the shoulders, big drooping ears and a fold of loose skin under the neck called a dewlap.

Those features help them cope with heat. Loose skin gives off more warmth, and zebu [[@sweat|sweat]] more than European cattle. They also put up better with ticks, flies and dry, poor grass.

Zebu were tamed from wild cattle called aurochs, near the Indus valley, more than 8,000 years ago. A few thousand years later, seals from the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]] were carved with proud humped bulls.

In Hindu tradition, Krishna is often called Gopala, the protector of cows. Shiva rides a bull named Nandi, whose statues sit facing many Shiva temples. [[@myths-indian-creatures|Kamadhenu]], a wish-granting cow, appears in old stories.

Festivals honour cattle too. During [[@onam-pongal|Pongal]] in Tamil Nadu, one day is Mattu Pongal, when cattle are washed, their horns painted and garlanded. In Maharashtra, [[@people-farmers-day|farmers celebrate their bullocks]] at the festival of Pola. Many states have laws protecting cows, though these laws differ from state to state.

Indian cattle have travelled the world. In the 1800s and early 1900s, ranchers in the USA brought zebu cattle from India, including Gir, Ongole and Kankrej. In [[@texas|Texas]], they crossed them with other cattle to make the Brahman breed, which handles the hot, humid Gulf Coast well.

In Brazil, Ongole cattle from Andhra Pradesh became the Nelore, now the country's most common beef breed. Gir cows from Gujarat have become important dairy cattle there too.

In the 1970s, India launched Operation Flood, which linked village dairy cooperatives to cities. It was led by Verghese Kurien and grew out of the [[@amul|Amul]] cooperative in Anand, Gujarat. By the late 1990s India had become the largest milk producer in the world, a story told in the [[@white-revolution|White Revolution]].

Village life has changed since then. Tractors have replaced many bullocks. Farmers often prefer crossbred cows that give more milk, so some native breeds have become rare. The government and breeders are now working to protect them, because those heat-hardy Indian cattle may matter even more in a warming world.

text: Earthworms turn dead stuff into good [[@soil-made|soil]]. They pull fallen leaves and plant scraps down into their burrows and eat them, along with mouthfuls of soil. What comes out the other end, called castings, is rich in nutrients that plants can easily use.

Their [[@tunnels|tunnels]] help too. They let air and rainwater soak deep into the ground, so roots can grow and breathe, and the soil doesn't wash away so easily in heavy rain. As worms burrow, they mix the soil, bringing deep earth up and carrying surface leaves down.

A field with lots of earthworms is usually a healthy field. That is why [[@people-farmers-day|farmers in India]] and around the world call them the farmer's friend, and why some make [[compost|compost]] with them.

st.reveal: Oxygen passes straight through a worm's thin, damp skin into its blood. That only works while the skin stays moist, so worms hide from hot sun and dry air. A worm stranded on a hot path can dry out and die.

sec.t:
An earthworm is a long tube of rings called segments. Tiny bristles on each segment grip the soil, and muscles squeeze and stretch the body, pushing the worm forward like a wave.

It has no eyes, but its skin can sense light, and it quickly wriggles away from bright sun. It has no [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] either. It breathes through its skin, which must stay damp. Instead of one heart, it has five pairs of pumping tubes near its front end.

Each worm is both male and female. The pale band partway along the body makes a little case for the eggs, which is left in the soil to hatch.

Charles Darwin is famous for his ideas about evolution, but he also loved earthworms. For about forty years he studied them in his garden and in pots in his house in England.

He tested whether worms could hear by playing a whistle, a bassoon and the [[@piano|piano]] to them. They ignored the music. But when he set their pots on top of the piano and struck a note, the worms dived for cover. They felt the vibration.

He also measured how fast worms buried stones, ancient ruins and anything left on the surface. His last book, published in 1881, was all about worms. It showed that these small animals reshape the land over time.

{{story:soil-made}}

After heavy rain, worms often crawl out onto paths and roads. People used to think they were escaping drowning. But worms can survive under water for a long time.

Scientists now have other ideas. Damp ground may make it safe for worms to travel across the surface to new places. The drumming of raindrops may also feel like a mole digging, which sends worms fleeing upwards.

In Florida, in the USA, people collect fishing worms by rubbing a wooden stake driven into the ground, a practice called worm grunting. In 2008, a scientist showed that the buzzing feels to worms like a hungry mole, so they wriggle up to escape.

Many Indian farmers and households now practise vermicomposting. They feed kitchen scraps, dung and crop waste to worms in pits or tanks. Within weeks, the worms turn it into dark, crumbly [[@compost|compost]] for fields and gardens.

It is a cheap way to make fertiliser and to deal with [[@food-waste|food waste]]. The red wiggler, a small worm that loves rotting food, is a favourite.

In the northern USA and Canada, ice sheets scraped away the native worms during the last [[@ice-ages|Ice Age]]. For thousands of years, forests there grew without earthworms. A thick, spongy carpet of fallen leaves built up on the forest floor.

Then settlers brought worms from Europe, in soil around plants and in ships. These worms eat the leaf carpet quickly, which harms wildflowers, salamanders and birds that depend on it. In a vegetable patch they help. In those forests, scientists treat them as invaders.

text: Many of the foods we eat come from flowers that need [[pollen|pollen]] carried from one flower to another. That job is done by pollinators. Most are insects, especially bees, but flies, butterflies, moths, beetles, birds and even bats help too. They visit flowers for sweet [[nectar|nectar]] or protein-rich pollen and get dusted with pollen as they feed.

A 2016 global report found that more than three-quarters of the leading kinds of food crops benefit at least partly from animal pollinators. Rice, wheat and maize mostly don't need them, because wind or the plant itself does the job. But many fruits, vegetables, nuts, oils and spices do.

myth: Honeybees do almost all the pollinating.

Honeybees are important farm pollinators, but there are about 20,000 kinds of bees, plus flies, butterflies, moths, beetles, birds and bats. Wild pollinators do a large share of the work, and for some crops they do better than honeybees.

sec.t:
There are about 20,000 kinds of bees in the world. Honeybees are the best known because people keep them in hives. India has several native honeybees, including the giant rock bee, which builds huge hanging combs on cliffs, trees and even city buildings.

Most bees don't live in hives at all. Many are solitary, nesting alone in tiny holes in the ground or in hollow stems. Bumblebees can "buzz pollinate", shaking their flight muscles so hard that pollen falls out of flowers like tomatoes and aubergines. Honeybees can't do this.

In the United States, California's almond orchards need so many bees that beekeepers truck in well over a million hives each spring. In India, apple growers in [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]] often rent hives during flowering, because a good [[@apples|apple]] needs plenty of bee visits.

[[@food-vanilla|Vanilla]] comes from the pod of an orchid native to Mexico. People took vanilla plants to other tropical lands, but the flowers rarely made pods. The bees that pollinate it in Mexico weren't there.

In 1841, on the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean, an enslaved 12-year-old boy named Edmond Albius found a solution. Using a thin stick and his thumb, he could pollinate a vanilla flower by hand in seconds. His method spread across the world and is still used today. Albius gained his freedom when [[@slavery-freedom|slavery was abolished]] on Réunion in 1848, but he received little reward for his discovery.

Pollinators face many problems: loss of wild flowers, pesticides, diseases and a changing climate. Anyone can help a little. Planting native flowers, leaving patches of bare soil for ground-nesting bees and keeping a shallow dish of water with pebbles all give them a boost. Even a few pots of flowers on a balcony can feed visiting bees.

[[@people-farmers-day|Farmers]] can help too, by leaving hedges and strips of wild flowers between fields. In parts of China where wild bees became scarce, some apple and pear growers have had to pollinate blossoms by hand, with brushes and feathers. It is slow, costly work, and it shows how much free help pollinators normally give.

text: Water is made of tiny [[molecule|molecules]] that are always moving and bumping into each other. Heating water makes them move faster. At the bottom of a pan, the water closest to the flame gets hottest. When it reaches its boiling point, some molecules move so fast that they break free of their neighbours and become a gas, called water vapour or steam.

That gas forms [[@bubbles-round|bubbles]] at the bottom of the pan. The bubbles are lighter than the water around them, so they rise, burst at the surface and release the steam into the air. At sea level this happens at 100°C. As long as the water keeps boiling, it stays at that temperature, even if you turn the flame up.

st.prompt: A pot of water has been boiling for five minutes on a high flame. What is its temperature now?
st.reveal: Once water is boiling, extra heat goes into turning water into steam, not into making the water hotter. So an open pot at sea level stays at about 100°C however high the flame. A bigger flame just makes it boil away faster.

d.try: Fill a clear glass with cold water from the fridge and leave it on a table for an hour. Look closely at the inside of the glass. Tiny bubbles will have formed on the sides. They are air that was dissolved in the cold water and comes out as the water warms, the same bubbles you see first when a pot starts heating.
myth: Adding salt to water makes it boil much faster.

Salt actually raises the boiling point very slightly, so salty water has to get a little hotter before it boils. With the pinch people add for cooking, the difference is far too small to notice. Cooks add salt for flavour.

sec.t:
If you watch a pan heating up, you'll see things happen in order. First come tiny bubbles that cling to the sides. These are air, which was dissolved in the water and comes out as the water warms.

Next comes a hissing or singing sound. Steam bubbles are forming on the hot bottom, then collapsing as they rise into cooler water above. Each collapse makes a tiny crackle. Once all the water is hot enough, the steam bubbles survive the trip to the top and the water rolls and churns. That is a full boil.

Water boils when its molecules can push back against the air pressing down on the surface. At sea level, the weight of all the air above is fairly heavy. High up a mountain there is less air on top, so the water molecules escape more easily and the water boils at a lower temperature.

In Leh, in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], about 3,500 metres up, water boils at around 88°C. On top of [[@mountaineering|Everest]] it boils at about 70°C. Water that boils at a lower temperature cooks food more slowly, so dal and rice take much longer. That's why people in high places rely on the [[@pressure-cooker|pressure cooker]], which raises the pressure and lets water get hotter before it boils.

When water turns to steam, it spreads out to take up about 1,600 times more room. Trap that steam in a closed space and it pushes very hard. This push drove the [[@steam-engine|steam engines]] that powered factories, ships and the first railways in the 1800s, including India's first passenger train in 1853.

Boiling also makes water safer to drink. Keeping water at a rolling boil for a minute kills most of the germs that cause illness. Steam is hotter than it looks, though, and a jet of it can scald skin badly, so kettles and cookers are best left to adults.

text: No. If there is no air in the way, everything falls at exactly the same speed. Heavy things are pulled harder by [[gravity|gravity]], but they are also harder to get moving. The two effects cancel out.
On Earth, air pushes back on falling things. A feather is light and spread out, so air slows it a lot. That's why a feather floats down while a hammer drops.
Near Earth's surface, gravity makes any falling thing speed up by about 9.8 metres per second, every second, if air doesn't get in the way.

st.reveal: Gravity speeds up all objects at the same rate. Air pushes back a little, which matters for light, spread-out things like feathers, but not much for two balls.

d.try: Drop a coin and a flat sheet of paper together from the same height. The coin wins. Now scrunch the paper into a tight ball and drop them again. They should land at almost the same moment. The paper didn't get heavier; it just has less air to push aside.
myth: Astronauts float in the space station because there is no gravity in space.

At the height of the space station, gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are falling around Earth together, so nothing pushes against them.

sec.t:
In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the Moon, where there is almost no air. They hit the ground at the same moment. A TV camera filmed it, and you can still watch the clip. Scott joked that it showed [[@galileo|Galileo]] had been right.

Gravity on the Moon is only about a sixth of Earth's, so both fell slowly. But they fell slowly together.

For nearly 2,000 years, many people followed the Greek thinker Aristotle, who taught that heavy things fall faster. About 400 years ago, the Italian scientist Galileo argued that falling objects speed up at the same rate. There's a famous story that he dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. We don't know if he really did.

What he certainly did was roll balls down long, gentle ramps and time them, sometimes with a water [[@clocks|clock]]. Slowing the fall down let him measure it. He found that the distance grew with the square of the time, whatever the ball's weight.

Isaac Newton realised that the same force pulling an apple down also keeps the Moon going around Earth. He published his law of gravity in 1687. It says every object pulls on every other object, and the pull gets weaker with distance.

The Moon is falling towards Earth all the time. It's just moving sideways so fast that it keeps missing.

The pull works both ways. The Moon tugs on Earth too, heaving the oceans into gentle bulges that give coasts from Gujarat to Maine their rising and falling [[@tides|tides]].

{{story:newton-life}}

Long before Newton, thinkers in many places wondered why things fall. The Indian mathematician [[@brahmagupta|Brahmagupta]], writing in the 600s, is often credited with saying that the Earth attracts objects towards itself. He didn't have Newton's mathematics, but he saw falling as a pull from the Earth.

You don't have to go to the Moon to see the hammer test. NASA has a huge vacuum chamber in Ohio, big enough to hold a whole spacecraft. In 2014, scientists pumped out nearly all its air for a TV programme, then dropped a bowling ball and a bunch of feathers. The feathers didn't drift or flutter. They fell like stones, exactly alongside the ball.

Astronauts on the [[@space-station|space station]] aren't floating because gravity has switched off. They're falling, just like the Moon, always around Earth and never into it. Skydivers feel something similar for a moment before the air slows them to a steady speed of about 200 km/h. Open a parachute, and its wide canopy catches so much air that the speed drops to a gentle landing, the feather trick on a human scale.

text: When you talk, your voice pushes the air in quick little waves. A microphone has a very thin sheet inside, called a diaphragm, that wobbles back and forth when those waves hit it. The microphone then turns each wobble into a tiny change in electric current.

A big, fast wobble makes a big change in current, and a small one makes a small change. So the electrical signal has the same shape as the sound. That signal can be made louder, sent down a wire, stored on a phone or beamed across the world, and a speaker at the other end can turn it back into sound.

st.prompt: What do the wobbling part of a microphone and the inside of your ear have in common?

options.t: Both use a thin, springy sheet that shakes when sound hits it
Both are filled with liquid that splashes

st.reveal: Your eardrum and a microphone's diaphragm are both thin sheets that wobble in and out as sound waves push on them. Your ear passes the wobble to tiny bones and nerves. A microphone turns it into a changing electric current.

d.try: Stretch cling film tightly over a bowl and sprinkle a few grains of rice or salt on top. Hold a metal plate near it and tap the plate, or hum loudly close to the bowl. Watch the grains jump as the sound makes the film shake, just like the diaphragm inside a microphone.
myth: The loud squeal you sometimes hear at school events means the microphone is broken.

That howl is called feedback. Sound from the speaker reaches the microphone, gets made louder, comes out of the speaker again and loops round faster and faster. Moving the microphone away from the speaker or turning it down usually stops it.
facts: turns sound vibrations into an electrical signal

sec.t:
Microphones copy something your body already does. Your eardrum is a thin skin that shakes when [[@sound-travel|sound waves]] arrive. Behind it, tiny bones and hair cells in [[@ears-hear|your ear]] turn the shaking into nerve signals for your brain. A microphone's diaphragm plays the eardrum's part, and wires do the job of nerves.

The trick is in how the shaking becomes electricity. There are three common ways.

A **dynamic microphone** has a small coil of wire glued to the diaphragm, sitting next to a magnet. When the coil moves, the magnet makes a current flow in it. This is the same rule that makes power stations work. Dynamic microphones are tough, which is why singers on stage and reporters in the rain often use them.

A **condenser microphone** uses a diaphragm that acts as one of two metal plates very close together. As the gap changes, the electric charge between the plates changes too. These microphones need a little power, but they catch quiet sounds and fine detail, so recording studios love them.

A **MEMS microphone** is a condenser shrunk onto a silicon chip just a few millimetres across. Your phone, earbuds and smart speakers use these. Many phones have two to four of them, and they compare what each one hears to cancel out traffic and wind.

{{story:ears-hear}}

Not every microphone listens in every direction. Some pick up sound equally from all around, which suits a meeting table. Many stage microphones mostly hear what is in front of them and ignore sound from behind, so a singer's voice comes through but the band's speakers don't. Engineers call this pattern "cardioid", from the Greek for heart, because a map of where it listens looks heart-shaped.

Film crews use long, thin "shotgun" microphones on poles held just out of the camera's view. These hear a narrow beam of sound, so an actor's whisper can be caught from a few metres away. At football matches, operators point dish-shaped reflectors at the pitch to catch the thud of a kick.

The first useful microphones came with the [[@telephone|telephone]] in the 1870s. Inventors such as Emile Berliner, Thomas Edison and David Edward Hughes found that loose grains of carbon changed how well they carried electricity when sound squeezed them. Carbon microphones were crackly, but they worked well enough to sit in telephones for about a hundred years.

Today microphones turn up in odd places. In international cricket, a microphone hidden in the stumps, called the stump mic, picks up the faint click of a ball brushing a bat. Hospitals use tiny microphones in digital stethoscopes. [[@voice-assistants|Voice assistants]] keep a microphone listening for one wake word before they start recording.

A dynamic microphone and a small [[@loudspeakers|speaker]] are built almost the same way: a coil, a magnet and something that wobbles. Push electricity in, and the speaker moves air. Push air at it, and it makes electricity. That is why old wired headphones can work, weakly, as a microphone. It is also why some walkie-talkies use one part for both jobs.

text: A coin rolls down a short track inside the machine, and on the way it is tested several times. Gaps and slots check that it is the right size and thickness. A sensor checks its weight. Then comes the clever part: [[@magnets-how|magnets]] and electric coils check what metal it is made of.

Every kind of coin is made of a particular mix of metals, called an [[alloy|alloy]]. Each alloy reacts to magnetic fields in its own way, almost like a fingerprint. If all the tests match a real coin, a little gate flips and sends the coin into the cash box. If not, the gate sends it to the return slot.

d.try: Collect a few different coins. Line them up by size with a ruler, then weigh them on a kitchen scale if you have one. Finally, hold a fridge magnet near each. Some will stick and some won't, and a vending machine notices all three differences.
myth: If a snack gets stuck, rocking or shaking the machine is a harmless way to get it out.
Vending machines are very heavy, often several hundred kilograms. Machines rocked by people have tipped over and caused serious injuries. It's safer to tell the owner.

sec.t:
The idea is very old. Hero of Alexandria, an engineer in Roman Egypt, described a coin machine in the 1st century CE. A visitor dropped a bronze coin into a slot at a temple. The coin fell onto a little tray attached to a lever. Its weight tipped the lever, which opened a valve, and holy water trickled out. When the coin slid off the tray, the lever sprang back and the water stopped.

Coin machines came back in the 1800s. In London in the 1880s, machines sold postcards. Soon there were machines selling chewing gum in New York and chocolate in railway stations.

Many coins aren't magnetic at all, yet magnets can still test them. When a metal coin moves past a strong magnet, tiny swirls of electric current form inside the coin. These currents push back against the magnet and slow the coin down.

How much it slows depends on the metal. Copper slows a lot, while some steel and nickel alloys behave very differently. Some coins also stick to the magnet. A sensor times the coin as it passes, and a fake made of the wrong metal moves at the wrong speed. A [[@metal-detectors|metal detector]] uses a similar trick to find coins buried in sand.

Modern machines often use electric coils instead of fixed magnets. The coil sends out a magnetic field and measures how the coin changes it. A small computer compares the result with a stored list of real coins.

{{story:metal-detectors}}

Paper money is harder to check. A note reader pulls the note in with rollers and shines light through it and onto it. [[sensor|Sensors]] look at the patterns, the watermark and the size. Many notes, including Indian rupees, have special inks and security threads that react to ultraviolet light or magnets. If anything looks wrong, the rollers push the note back out.

Japan is famous for its vending machines. Even in 2025, after years of decline, it had close to 2 million machines selling drinks alone. Some serve hot soup, umbrellas or fresh eggs. Part of the reason is that crime is low, so machines can stand on quiet street corners without being broken open.

In India, vending machines have spread in a different way. Railway stations have ticket machines, and offices have tea and coffee machines. Many newer machines barely bother with coins. You scan a QR code and pay with [[@upi-payments|UPI]] on your phone, and the machine checks with the bank before dropping your snack.

A good vending machine has to be honest both ways. It must reject fake coins, but it mustn't swallow real ones. Coins get scratched, dented and dirty over years, so engineers allow a little wiggle room in every test. When a country brings out a new coin, machine owners have to update their checkers, or the machines will refuse it.

text: India's great stone temples were built by teams of architects, stone carvers, labourers and artists, often working for decades. They followed design rules written in old texts called the Shilpa Shastras, which set out how to plan a temple, how big each part should be and where the images should go.

Builders cut stone from quarries, moved it with ramps, rollers, levers, ropes and animals, and fitted blocks together, often without any mortar. Carvers then covered the walls with gods, dancers, animals and patterns. Many temples are still in daily use, so they are working places of worship as well as great works of art.

This is a popular story, but it isn't true. Like every tall building, the tower casts a shadow whenever the sun shines. Its broad base means the shadow at noon mostly falls on the temple itself.

sec.t:
Temple builders often started with a square grid called a *mandala*, a plan that represents the order of the universe. The centre square is where the main deity sits.

That central room is the *garbhagriha*, meaning womb-chamber. It's usually small, dark and plain. Above it rises the tallest tower. In front are one or more halls, called mandapas, where people gather. Moving inward from the bright entrance to the dim shrine is meant to feel like a journey towards the sacred.

The [[@india-wonder-brihadeeswara|Brihadeeswarar temple]] in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu, was completed around 1010 CE by the Chola king Rajaraja I. Its vimana rises about 66 metres, as tall as a 20-storey building, and it was the tallest temple in India when it was built.

It is built of granite, a very hard stone. The blocks were cut to fit tightly and held in place largely by their own weight and by careful interlocking. At the very top sits a huge capstone, often said to weigh around 80 tonnes. Nobody wrote down exactly how it was raised. One popular idea is a long earth ramp; others suggest scaffolding and [[@lever-lift|levers]] used in stages.

Once the structure was up, carvers brought the walls to life. They carved gods and goddesses, guardians at the doors, musicians, dancers, elephants and scenes from the epics. At Thanjavur, wall paintings from the Chola period were later found hidden under newer paintings.

Some temples were not built at all but carved downwards out of solid rock, like the Kailasa temple at Ellora, described in [[@ellora-kailasa|How was the Kailasa temple carved from one rock?]].

A big temple was more than a place of prayer. It employed priests, musicians, dancers, cooks, gardeners and accountants. It owned land, stored grain and hosted festivals. Towns often grew around temples, with streets circling them in rings.

Rulers built grand temples partly to show their power and devotion. The [[@cholas|Cholas]] carved long inscriptions on their temple walls listing gifts, names and even the wages of temple staff, which tell historians a great deal about life a thousand years ago.

text: A tabla is a pair of hand drums. The smaller, wooden drum on the right, the *dayan*, plays crisp, ringing notes. The bigger drum on the left, the *bayan*, made of metal or clay, plays deep, booming sounds.

Both drums have a black circle on their skin called the *syahi*. This heavy paste makes the skin vibrate in a special way, so the drum produces a clear musical note instead of a dull thud. A player strikes different parts of the skin with different fingers, and each spot makes its own sound. Mix them, and the tabla seems to have a hundred voices.

st.prompt: What is the black circle on a tabla made of?

options.t: A paste of iron filings, soot and flour, built up in layers

st.reveal: The syahi is pressed on in many thin layers, each rubbed smooth with a stone. Its extra weight in the middle of the skin changes how the drum vibrates, so it rings with a clear note.

Britannica, Tabla.
n.certNote: How the tabla works is well understood. Where it came from is not. A popular story credits the poet Amir Khusrau, but historians find no evidence for it, and most think the tabla took shape in the 1700s.

d.try: Stretch a piece of balloon tightly over the mouth of an empty tin and fix it with a rubber band. Tap the centre and then near the edge. Now stick a small blob of play dough in the middle and tap again. Listen for how the extra weight changes the sound.
myth: The poet Amir Khusrau invented the tabla in the 1200s.
This is a popular story, but no writing from his time mentions the tabla. Most historians think it developed in the 1700s, partly from an older barrel drum called the pakhawaj.

sec.t:
Tabla players learn their sounds as spoken syllables called *bols*. "Na" is a sharp ring from the rim of the right drum. "Ge" is a deep boom on the left. "Dha" is both together. Students recite whole patterns aloud before they ever play them.

Rhythm patterns follow [[@maths-music-rhythm|cycles]] called *taal*. The most common, *teentaal*, has 16 beats grouped as 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. The first beat, *sam*, is the strongest, and musicians often finish a dazzling passage exactly on it. You can learn to clap teentaal in [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]].

The left drum can do something surprising. By pressing the heel of the hand into the skin and sliding it, a player makes the pitch swoop up or down, a bit like a voice saying "whoa". This sliding sound gives the tabla its playful, talking quality.

The right drum is tuned to a particular note, usually the main note of the song. Players tap small wooden blocks under the leather straps with a little hammer to tighten or loosen the skin until it matches.

A favourite story says the tabla was invented in the 1200s by Amir Khusrau, a poet at the [[@delhi|court of Delhi]]. Historians doubt it. No written record from his time mentions the instrument. The tabla probably grew from the older *pakhawaj* and other drums, and became popular in the 1700s as lighter music suited it better.

Different teaching families, called *gharanas*, grew up in Delhi, Lucknow, Banaras, [[@punjab|Punjab]] and elsewhere. Each has its own favourite strokes and pieces, passed down from teacher to student.

The tabla accompanies singers, sitar players and dancers of [[@kathak|Kathak]]. It is also heard in countless Hindi [[@film-songs|film songs]].

Ustad Alla Rakha toured the world with the sitar player [[@ravi-shankar|Ravi Shankar]] in the 1960s. His son, Zakir Hussain, became one of the most famous tabla players ever. He lived for many years in California, played with musicians from jazz to rock, and won several Grammy awards before his death in 2024. Thanks to them, children in [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] can now learn the same bols as children in Kolkata.

text: Euclid was a Greek mathematician who lived around 300 BCE in Alexandria, a great city in Egypt. He wrote the Elements, a book that collected the geometry and number knowledge of his time and arranged it into a clear chain of proofs.

The Elements starts with a few simple definitions and assumptions, then proves hundreds of results step by step, each built on the ones before. It was copied, translated and taught for more than 2,000 years. The geometry you learn about triangles, [[@circles|circles]] and parallel lines at school is still called Euclidean geometry.

st.reveal: Lincoln wrote in 1860 that he had studied and nearly mastered the first six books of Euclid after serving in Congress. He wanted to understand what "demonstrate", or prove, really meant, so he could make stronger arguments in court.

Euclid gathered and organised the work of earlier Greek mathematicians, such as Eudoxus and Theaetetus, and added proofs of his own. His great achievement was arranging it all in a clear, logical order, starting from a few simple assumptions.

sec.t:
We know almost nothing about Euclid as a person. He probably taught in Alexandria, which the rulers of Egypt had turned into a centre of learning with a famous library. Scholars came from all over the Greek world to study at the [[@great-libraries|great library]] there.

A story written about 700 years later says that King Ptolemy asked Euclid for a shortcut to learning geometry. Euclid is said to have replied that there is no royal road to geometry. It is a good story, but nobody knows if it really happened.

In Book IX, Euclid proved that [[@prime-numbers|prime numbers]] never run out. His argument goes like this. Suppose you had a complete list of primes. Multiply them all together and add 1. The new number cannot be divided exactly by any prime on your list, so either it is prime itself, or it has a prime factor missing from the list. Either way, the list was not complete.

He also described a step-by-step method for finding the highest common factor of two numbers by repeatedly subtracting or dividing. It is one of the oldest algorithms still in use. Computers use it today, including in some of the maths that protects online data.

Euclid's fifth postulate, about parallel lines, was longer and less obvious than the others. For centuries, mathematicians tried to prove it from the first four and failed. In the 1800s, several mathematicians, including Nikolai Lobachevsky in Russia and János Bolyai in Hungary, showed that you could build a consistent geometry where it is not true. These non-Euclidean geometries later helped [[@einstein|Einstein]] describe curved space.

The Elements was translated into Arabic, then into Latin, and was one of the first maths books ever printed, in [[@venice|Venice]] in 1482. In the United States, [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] studied the first six books as a young lawyer in the 1850s, to sharpen his reasoning.

In India, the ruler of [[@jaipur|Jaipur]], Sawai Jai Singh II, loved astronomy and built huge stone observatories. In the 1700s his court astronomer, Jagannatha Samrat, translated the Elements from Arabic into [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] under the name Rekhaganita. In 2023 the European Space Agency launched a space telescope named Euclid, to map billions of [[@galaxies|galaxies]] and study the shape of the universe.

text: Nature is full of repeating shapes. Sunflower seeds sit in spirals. Tigers and zebras wear stripes. Leopards and cheetahs have spots. Bees build hexagons. Trees, rivers and [[@lightning|lightning]] branch again and again. Sand dunes and the sea form waves.

These patterns aren't painted on by design. They grow out of simple rules. Things push and pull, spread and stop, crack and shrink, and the same shapes keep appearing because they are the easiest or most efficient result. That is why mathematicians, physicists and biologists all study them.

st.prompt: When thick lava cools slowly, it can crack into tall stone columns. What shape are most of them?
st.reveal: As lava cools it shrinks and cracks. The cracks tend to meet at about 120 degrees, which naturally makes hexagons, though five- and seven-sided columns turn up too. The same thing happens, on a smaller scale, in drying mud.

n.certNote: Scientists understand the maths behind many natural patterns. For some, like the exact way stripes form on certain animals, research is still going on and there may be more than one cause.

A zebra's skin underneath its fur is dark. Its stripes form where the hair cells make pigment or don't, so scientists usually describe a zebra as dark with white stripes. Why zebras have stripes at all is still being studied.

sec.t:
[[@alan-turing|Alan Turing]] is famous for helping to crack German codes during the Second World War, and for early ideas about computers. In 1952 he published a paper about something quite different: how living things get their patterns.

He imagined two chemicals spreading through a growing animal's skin. One switches on colour and also switches on more of itself. The other spreads faster and switches the first one off. Working through the maths, Turing showed that two such chemicals, left alone, could form spots or stripes all by themselves.

At the time there was little evidence. Decades later, biologists found this kind of process at work in the stripes of zebrafish and in the ridges inside a mouse's mouth. Scientists still debate how much it explains [[@tiger-stripes|tiger stripes]] and other coats, but Turing's idea is now a major part of the story.

{{story:tiger-stripes}}

When thick lava from a [[@volcano|volcano]] cools slowly, it shrinks. As it shrinks, it cracks. The cracks spread down into the rock and meet each other, often at angles of about 120 degrees. That makes tall columns, many of them six-sided.

The most famous are at the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland, with about 40,000 columns. In the United States, Devils Tower in Wyoming is a huge stump of them. India has its own: the St Mary's Islands, near Udupi in [[@karnataka|Karnataka]]. Their columns formed around 88 million years ago, when India was breaking away from [[@madagascar|Madagascar]]. They are a national geological monument.

Look at the middle of a sunflower and you'll see [[@maths-nature-shells|two sets of spirals]], one turning clockwise and one anticlockwise. Count them and you often get neighbouring numbers in the Fibonacci sequence: 34 and 55, or 55 and 89.

This happens because each new seed grows at a fixed angle from the last, about 137.5 degrees. That angle packs seeds tightly with no wasted gaps. Pine cones, pineapples and the leaves on many plants follow the same rule, as you can read in [[@fibonacci-nature|Fibonacci in nature]].

Rivers split into streams, which split into smaller streams. Trees split into branches and twigs. Your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] split into airways, then smaller ones, then tiny air sacs. Lightning forks across the sky.

Branching is a good way to reach every part of a big space from a single starting point. Each small part looks a little like the whole, a property that mathematicians call self-similarity. Shapes like these are known as [[@fractals|fractals]].

Wind blowing across sand piles it into ripples, and on a bigger scale into dunes. In the [[@desert-life|Thar Desert]], dunes march slowly across the land in rows. On a [[@beaches|beach]], ripples in wet sand form where the water flows back and forth.

Even a [[@snowflake-six|snowflake]] is a pattern made by simple rules, with six arms that grow as water molecules lock into ice. The same few shapes keep turning up, in stone and in skin, because nature keeps following the same few rules.

text: The Tower of Hanoi is a puzzle with three pegs and a stack of discs, each smaller than the one below it. Your job is to move the whole stack from one peg to another. You may move only one disc at a time, and you may never put a bigger disc on top of a smaller one.

With three discs, the best you can do is 7 moves. Add a disc and the moves more than double, to 15. Ten discs need 1,023 moves. The pattern is simple to write down: multiply 2 by itself once for each disc, then subtract 1. Mathematicians write it as 2ⁿ − 1, and it grows astonishingly fast.

st.prompt: Three discs take 7 moves. How many moves does it take to move 6 discs?
st.reveal: Each extra disc roughly doubles the work. The rule is 2 multiplied by itself once per disc, minus 1. For 6 discs that's 64 minus 1, which is 63.

myth: The Tower of Hanoi is an ancient puzzle from Vietnam or India.
It was invented in France in 1883 by Édouard Lucas. He made up the legend of the temple and the golden discs to sell his puzzle, and the name Hanoi was chosen to sound far away.
facts: Rule for any number of discs
2 to the power of discs, minus 1
Time for 64 discs at one move a second

sec.h: A puzzle with a made-up legend
sec.t:
The puzzle was invented in 1883 by Édouard Lucas, a French mathematician who loved games. He sold it as a toy, under the playful fake name "Professor N. Claus of Siam", which is a jumble of the letters in "Lucas d'Amiens".

To make it exciting, the box told a story. In a great temple at Benares, today's [[@varanasi|Varanasi]], priests were moving 64 golden discs between three diamond needles, following the same rules. When they finished, the world would crumble to dust. The temple never existed, but the story stuck.

sec.h: The trick: solve a smaller puzzle first
Why the priests will never finish
sec.t:
Every extra disc doubles the moves and adds one. That's the power of [[@exponents|exponents]]. For 64 discs, the total is 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 moves, more than 18 quintillion.

Suppose the priests never sleep, never slip and move one disc every second. They'd need about 585 billion years. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, so they'd need roughly 42 universe-lifetimes. Even a computer making a billion moves a second would take more than 580 years.

You can check the doubling yourself. One disc takes 1 move. Two discs take 3. Three take 7, four take 15 and five take 31. Each answer is double the one before, plus one. That's because moving a stack means moving the smaller stack on top of it twice, once out of the way and once back, with one big move in between.

By ten discs you've passed a thousand moves. By twenty, you're past a million.

The puzzle is full of surprises. In the fastest solution, the smallest disc moves on every other turn, always going around the pegs in the same direction. And if you number the moves 1, 2, 3 and so on, you can predict each one by writing its number in [[@binary-code|binary]], the 0-and-1 code used by computers. Count the zeros at the end: no zeros means the smallest disc moves, one zero means the next smallest, and so on.

Psychologists also use the puzzle to study how people plan ahead. And the strangest part? The same doubling that makes the priests' job impossible also ruined a king in an old tale, when he agreed to pay a reward in [[@puzzle-chessboard-rice|rice grains on a chessboard]].

sec.t:
Viswanathan Anand learned chess from his mother in [[@chennai|Chennai]], then called Madras. He played so fast as a teenager that he was nicknamed "the lightning kid". In 1988 he became India's first grandmaster, the highest title in chess.

He won his first world title in 2000 and became undisputed world champion in 2007, keeping the crown until 2013. Altogether he won five world championships. For a generation of Indian children, Anand showed that a player from India could beat anyone.

He was not the first Indian pioneer. Manuel Aaron, also from Tamil Nadu, became India's first International Master, the rank just below grandmaster, in 1961.

Koneru Humpy, from Andhra Pradesh, became a grandmaster in 2002 at 15, then the youngest woman ever to earn the title. She has won the women's world rapid championship twice, in 2019 and 2024.

In 2025 Divya Deshmukh of Nagpur, then 19, won the Women's World Cup, beating Humpy in an all-Indian final. The win also made her a grandmaster.

Inspired by Anand, thousands of Indian children joined chess clubs and online platforms. A wave of teenage grandmasters followed. Gukesh Dommaraju of Chennai won the Candidates Tournament in 2024 to earn a shot at the title.

In December 2024, in Singapore, he beat China's Ding Liren to become world champion at 18. Anand, by then mentoring young players at his own academy, had helped train many of them.

A few months earlier, at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest, India's open team of Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa, Arjun Erigaisi, Vidit Gujrathi and Pentala Harikrishna won gold. The women's team, including Harika Dronavalli, R. Vaishali and Divya Deshmukh, won gold too.

{{story:chess-india}}

Chennai has been called India's chess capital. Anand's success inspired local coaches, schools and clubs to take the game seriously. Gukesh and Praggnanandhaa grew up there, and in 2022 the Chess Olympiad was held at Mamallapuram, just south of the city.

[[@chess-online|Online chess]] also helped. During the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020 and 2021, huge numbers of Indian children started playing on phones and laptops, and many kept going.

Chess looks like pure calculation, but research suggests it is more about [[@memory|memory]] of patterns. In the 1970s psychologists showed that masters can glance at a real game and remember almost every piece, because they see familiar groups of pieces. They are no better than beginners with random boards.

Since 1997, when IBM's Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov, computers have been stronger than any human. Today's champions use [[@ai-what|artificial intelligence]] to prepare, testing millions of moves. Yet only a human champion feels the pressure of a world title match, playing for hours with nerves racing like a final over in cricket. Like the best [[@puzzles-logic|logic puzzles]], the game rewards patience as much as speed.

text: P.C. Sorcar, the most famous Indian magician of the 1900s, amazed audiences with huge stage illusions, a sense of drama and clever publicity. He dressed like a maharaja in a jewelled turban and silk robes, with a whole team of assistants. His show was called *Indrajal*, after an old word for magic.
Like all great magicians, he relied on misdirection, careful practice and hidden machinery. He turned Indian magic, once mostly done on street corners, into a big theatre show that toured the world.

Historians have found no reliable eyewitness account of the full trick. Its fame owes a lot to an 1890 Chicago newspaper story that was invented and later admitted to be a hoax.

sec.t:
Protul Chandra Sorcar was born in 1913 in Tangail, in Bengal, now part of Bangladesh. He studied mathematics but loved magic more. He practised for years and began performing in the 1930s.

At the time, Western audiences often saw Indian magic as small street tricks: snake charmers, mango trees that grew in minutes, cups and balls. Sorcar wanted something grander. He built a show with music, costumes, lights and big illusions, and took it to Europe, the USA, Japan and beyond. He won major magic awards in the USA and Germany, and in 1964 India gave him the Padma Shri.

Most magic works by controlling attention. Your brain cannot watch everything at once. When a magician looks at one hand, you look there too, while the other hand does the secret work. Magicians call this misdirection, and scientists who study [[@focus|focus]] have learnt a lot from them.

Stage illusions add hidden tools. Mirrors, black cloth against black backgrounds, false bottoms and special boxes make things seem to vanish or float. In the sawing trick, the "one" woman is often more than one person, or her body is safely folded somewhere you cannot see. Sorcar's team kept his secrets carefully, and many are still unknown.

sec.h: The rope trick that never was
sec.t:
The most famous "Indian" trick may never have been done at all. In the story, a fakir throws a rope into the air, where it stays stiff. A boy climbs up and disappears. In 1890, the *Chicago Tribune* printed a vivid report of the trick. Four months later, the paper admitted it was a hoax, but the story had already spread around the world.

Magicians searched India for decades and offered big prizes for a real performance. No one ever claimed the reward with the full trick. The story became a lesson in how a good tale can travel faster than the truth, much like [[@fake-news|fake news]] today.

Sorcar died in 1971 in Japan, just after a performance. His sons carried on. P.C. Sorcar Jr. became famous for illusions that seemed to make the Taj Mahal and a moving train vanish. Kolkata, his home city, has a street named after the elder Sorcar. Many of his tricks borrowed from the [[@circus|circus]] and theatre. And the reason his audiences never saw the secret move comes down to how easily the eye can be tricked, the science behind [[@optical-illusions|optical illusions]].

text: It depends on who you are. For growing children, especially those who might not get much food otherwise, breakfast clearly matters. It gives the body and brain fuel after a long night without food and helps children concentrate in class.

For adults, the picture is less clear. Scientists who have run careful experiments find that skipping breakfast doesn't make most healthy adults heavier or less healthy, as long as they eat well later.
So breakfast is important for many people, especially kids. Whether it's the *most* important meal is more slogan than science.

st.prompt: Researchers find that students who eat breakfast get better marks. Does that prove breakfast makes you cleverer?

options.t: Not on its own, because families who eat breakfast may differ in other ways too

st.reveal: This is the difference between correlation and cause. Children who eat breakfast might also sleep more or have more help at home. To prove breakfast itself helps, researchers have to give some children breakfast and compare them with similar children who don't get it.

n.certNote: Many studies find that children who eat breakfast do better at school, but most of these studies can't prove breakfast is the cause. For adults, trials have found that eating or skipping breakfast makes little difference to weight.

sec.t:
[[@brain-works|Your brain]] is a heavy user of energy. It makes up about 2 percent of your weight but burns about 20 percent of your energy. Its main fuel is glucose, a sugar your body makes from food.

Overnight, your body keeps using energy for breathing, repairs and dreams while you [[@sleep-why|sleep]]. By morning, it may have gone ten or twelve hours without food. Your [[@liver|liver]] releases stored glucose to keep the brain supplied, but those stores are limited. A meal tops them up.

Studies suggest that children who eat breakfast often find it easier to pay attention and remember things during morning lessons.

Hundreds of studies have compared people who eat breakfast with people who don't. Many find that breakfast-eaters are healthier and do better at school. But these studies have a problem: breakfast-eaters may also sleep more, exercise more or have more regular routines. Any of those could explain the difference.

Stronger evidence comes from trials, where researchers decide at random who eats breakfast. In 2019, a review of such trials in adults found that eating breakfast didn't help people lose weight. For children, trials of school breakfast programmes show benefits for attendance and attention, especially among children from poorer homes.

Because of this, many governments give children breakfast at school. The USA made its School Breakfast Program permanent in 1975, and millions of children now eat breakfast at school every day.

India's [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal scheme]] feeds about 11 crore children [[@lunch-world|lunch at school]] (2025 figure). In 2022, Tamil Nadu began giving free breakfast to young children in government schools, and some other states have tried similar ideas.

Nutrition experts say a good breakfast mixes different [[@food-nutrients|nutrients]]. Protein and fibre help you feel full for longer. Whole grains release energy slowly. Very sugary breakfasts can leave you hungry again soon.

Many traditional breakfasts already do well. A plate of [[@dosa-idli|idli and sambar]] combines fermented rice and [[@lentils-world|lentils]]. Poha with peanuts and vegetables, eggs with toast, or oats with fruit all work. In the end, a breakfast you enjoy and actually eat beats a perfect one you skip.

text: Grace Hopper was an American mathematician, computer scientist and US Navy officer. She was one of the first people to program a large computer, the Harvard Mark I, during the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]].

Her biggest idea was that people should be able to give computers instructions in words that look a little like English, instead of strings of numbers. She built one of the first compilers, programs that translate human-friendly code into the [[@binary-code|binary code]] a machine understands. That idea led to COBOL, a language still running in many [[@money-banks|banks]] and government offices today.

st.prompt: To show how far electricity travels in a billionth of a second, Grace Hopper handed out pieces of wire. About how long were they?
st.reveal: In one nanosecond, a billionth of a second, light travels about 30 centimetres, roughly the length of a school ruler. Hopper used the wires to explain why sending signals across long distances, even to a satellite, takes time.

myth: Grace Hopper invented the word "bug" for a computer problem.

Engineers, including Thomas Edison, were calling faults "bugs" in the 1800s. Hopper's team found a real moth in a computer in 1947 and joked about it in their logbook. She loved telling the story, which helped make the word famous.

sec.t:
Grace Brewster Murray was born in New York City in 1906. As a seven-year-old, she was so curious about how alarm clocks worked that she took apart several of them, one after another, until her mother limited her to one.

She studied maths and physics at Vassar College and earned a PhD in mathematics at Yale in 1934. That was rare for anyone at the time, and especially for a woman. She then taught maths at Vassar.

In 1947, the team working on the Mark II computer found it was making errors. Inside, they found a moth caught in one of its switches. They removed it and taped it into the logbook with a note that read "First actual case of bug being found".

The word "bug" was already in use for faults, but the story became famous. Hopper told it for the rest of her life. The logbook page, moth and all, is now kept at the [[@smithsonian|Smithsonian]]'s National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C.

In the early 1950s, most [[@programming|programming]] meant writing long lists of numbers. Hopper thought this was slow and full of mistakes. In 1952 her team built a compiler called A-0.

Many experts said computers could only do arithmetic, not understand words. Hopper proved them wrong with a language called FLOW-MATIC, which used English commands such as "compare" and "transfer". It helped inspire COBOL, created in 1959 by a group of companies and the US government. Hopper did not write COBOL alone, but she pushed hard for it and for computers that could share programs. She followed in a line that goes back to [[@ada-lovelace|Ada Lovelace]], who imagined computer programs a century earlier.

Hopper retired from the Navy several times, and was called back each time. When she finally left in 1986, aged 79, she was a rear admiral and the oldest serving officer in the US Navy.

She was famous for a clock in her office that ran backwards, to remind people that things do not have to be done the usual way. A Navy warship, USS Hopper, is named after her. In 2016 she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, one of America's highest honours. Today one of the world's largest gatherings of women in computing is named after her.

text: It depends on what "first" means. The first computer installed in India was the HEC-2M, a British-made machine set up at the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata in 1956. It was brought in by the statistician P. C. Mahalanobis to crunch survey data.

The first computer designed and built in India was TIFRAC, short for TIFR Automatic Calculator. A team at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai built it in the 1950s, and it was formally commissioned in 1960. Jawaharlal Nehru gave it its name. It filled a room, used about 2,700 vacuum tubes and could store just 2,048 numbers.

st.reveal: Vacuum tubes were early electronic switches. Each one could be on or off, which a computer reads as 1 or 0. Later, tiny transistors did the same job, and today one chip holds billions of them.

myth: India only started using computers in the 1980s or 1990s.

Indian scientists were using and building computers in the 1950s. Kolkata had an imported machine in 1956, and Mumbai's TIFRAC, built in India, was running by 1960, only about 15 years after the first electronic computers appeared.
facts: First designed and built in India

sec.t:
In Mumbai, the physicist [[@homi-bhabha|Homi Bhabha]] had a bolder idea. Instead of buying a computer, why not build one? A young team led by R. Narasimhan began work in 1955. They first made a small trial machine, which ran in 1956. Then they built the full computer, based on a famous design from Princeton in the USA.

India had almost no electronics industry then, so many parts had to be imported. The team then wired thousands of them together by hand. TIFRAC used about 2,700 vacuum tubes, 1,700 germanium diodes and some 12,500 resistors. Its memory was made of tiny rings of magnetic material called ferrite cores, then a new idea.

Each vacuum tube worked as a switch, on or off, standing for 1 or 0 in [[@binary-code|binary code]]. TIFRAC's memory held 2,048 "words", each 40 binary digits long. That adds up to roughly 10 kilobytes, less than one tiny photo on a phone.

Yet scientists queued to use it. TIFRAC solved problems in physics, engineering and statistics that would have taken people weeks of calculation. It stayed in use until around 1965, when newer imported machines took over.

Vacuum tubes glow like small light bulbs and get hot. A room full of them needed powerful cooling, and a single burnt-out tube could stop the whole machine until engineers tracked it down. Smaller, cooler and far more reliable transistors replaced them. In 1966, the Indian Statistical Institute and Jadavpur University in Kolkata finished ISIJU, an early Indian-built computer that used transistors instead of tubes.

Universities joined in. IIT Kanpur got an IBM 1620 in 1963 and began teaching students how to program it. Many of India's first computer scientists learned on that machine. Students wrote programs on paper, punched them onto cards, and sometimes waited hours for a result.

In the late 1980s, India wanted a supercomputer to forecast the monsoon. The USA, worried about how such machines might be used, would not sell its most powerful model. So India decided to build its own.

A new centre called C-DAC was set up in Pune in 1988, led by the scientist Vijay Bhatkar. In 1991 it unveiled PARAM 8000, which linked many processors to work together. It was India's first [[@supercomputers|supercomputer]]. Today the descendants of those machines help plan [[@isro-missions|ISRO missions]], forecast cyclones and design medicines.

text: Native American nations are the peoples who lived in North America long before Europeans arrived, and their descendants today. They are not one group. There are hundreds of nations, such as the Navajo, Cherokee, Lakota, Ojibwe and Hopi, each with its own language, history and way of life.

The United States recognises 575 of them as having their own governments, which can make many of their own laws. Many Native people live on reservations, but most live in towns and cities across the country. Together, about 9.7 million people identified as American Indian or Alaska Native in the 2020 US census, some of them alongside another heritage.

sec.t:
Before 1492, North America was home to a huge variety of cultures. In the Southwest, the ancestors of the Pueblo peoples built many-storey towns of stone and adobe. On the Pacific coast, nations carved tall cedar totem poles and caught salmon. In the Northeast, the Haudenosaunee lived in long bark houses and formed a league of nations that made decisions together.

Near today's St. Louis, a city called Cahokia grew around 1100 CE, with an earthen mound about as tall as a ten-storey building at its centre. At its peak it may have been home to more people than London at the time.

Farmers across the Americas also bred crops the whole world now eats. Maize, beans, squash, potatoes, tomatoes and [[@chillies|chillies]] all began as Native American crops. Without them, Indian cooking would look very different.

The word "Indian" came from [[@columbus|Columbus]], who thought he had reached the Indies in 1492. The name stuck. Today people use "Native American" or "American Indian", and many prefer the name of their own nation, such as Diné for the Navajo. In Canada, the term "First Nations" is common.

{{story:code-talkers}}

As European settlers spread west, Native nations lost most of their land through wars, broken treaties and forced moves. Diseases from Europe, such as [[@disease-history|smallpox]], had already killed huge numbers of people.

In 1830 the [[@congress-usa|US Congress]] passed the Indian Removal Act. Thousands of Cherokee, Muscogee, Choctaw and others were forced from the Southeast to land west of the [[@mississippi|Mississippi]]. The Cherokee call their 1838 march the Trail of Tears. Several thousand people died of cold, hunger and disease on the way. Later, many Native children were sent to boarding schools that tried to wipe out their languages and cultures.

Despite all this, Native nations survived. In the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], Navajo [[@code-talkers|Code Talkers]] used their language to send military messages that enemy forces never cracked. In 1924 all Native people born in the United States became citizens, although some states still blocked them from voting for decades.

Today nations run their own schools, hospitals and businesses. Many are working hard to teach their languages to children, because many have only a few elderly speakers left. The bison, once almost wiped out, are being brought back to Native lands by groups such as the InterTribal Buffalo Council.

Because of Columbus's mistake, Americans and Indians share a word that causes endless confusion. India has its own [[indigenous|Indigenous]] peoples too, the Adivasi communities, who numbered more than 10 crore in the 2011 census. Like Native Americans, many have fought to protect their forests, languages and land rights.

text: Life at an Antarctic research station is a mix of careful science, hard outdoor work and long days indoors with the same small group. Around 70 stations, run by about 30 countries, are spread across the ice. In summer the continent holds a few thousand people. In winter, only about a thousand stay on.

Everything has to be shipped or flown in, from fresh vegetables to fuel. Waste is carried out again. People sleep in heated rooms, eat in a shared dining hall and dress in several layers before stepping outside, where the wind can freeze bare skin in minutes.

st.prompt: Which of these do Antarctic stations have to be most careful about?

options.t: Fire, because the air is so dry and help is so far away

st.reveal: Antarctica is a desert, and its cold air holds almost no moisture, so wood and paper dry out completely. A fire in winter could destroy the only shelter for hundreds of kilometres. Stations run regular fire drills and keep spare buildings for emergencies.
