d.try: Fill two identical cups with warm water. Wrap one in a woolly sock or a few layers of cloth, and leave the other bare. Check them with your finger every ten minutes. Station buildings are built like the wrapped cup, with thick layers that trap warmth inside.
myth: Anyone who wants to can go and live in Antarctica.

Nobody lives there permanently. Almost everyone on the continent is a scientist or support worker sent by a national programme for a few months or a year, and the Antarctic Treaty says the land can be used only for peace and science.
facts: about 1,000 in winter, about 4,000 or more in summer

sec.t:
India's first station, Dakshin Gangotri, was set up in 1983 and was slowly buried by snow until it was closed. Maitri opened in 1989 beside a freshwater lake in an ice-free patch of rock. Bharati followed in 2012, on a rocky headland near the coast. It is made partly from shipping containers and looks a bit like a silver spaceship parked on a hill.

Each year an Indian expedition sails south from Goa or Cape Town. Some members stay only for the summer. A smaller winter team keeps the station running through the dark months, when no ship can get through the frozen sea. Doctors, cooks, engineers and radio operators go too, because a station is really a tiny village that has to fix its own pipes, generators and vehicles.

sec.h: Science you can only do here

sec.t:
At the South Pole, the Sun sets once a year and stays down for about six months. Stations nearer the coast get a few hours of dim light in midwinter. People keep to a strict timetable for meals and work, partly to keep their body clocks steady.

Cooking duty, cleaning and snow clearing are shared. Showers are often short, because water comes from melting snow, which takes fuel. Fresh fruit runs out early, so frozen and tinned food fills the menu. Birthdays and festivals become big events, and many stations celebrate Midwinter Day on 21 June with a special dinner. Some teams make their own films, hold quiz nights or grow lettuce and herbs under lamps in a small indoor garden. A few leaves of something green can feel like a feast after months of tinned peas.

The nearest hospital may be thousands of kilometres away, so most stations have a doctor, and everyone learns first aid. In winter, an emergency flight can be almost impossible. Teams practise fire drills often, because the air is so dry that a fire spreads fast.

Living with the same 20 or 25 people for months can be tough. Space agencies study winter crews to learn how astronauts on long missions to a [[@space-station|space station]] might cope with being shut in together.

Early visitors, like the [[@explorers-poles|explorers who raced to the Pole]] in 1911, came for glory. Today the rules are different. The Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959 and joined by India in 1983, bans military bases and nuclear tests, and a later agreement from 1991 bans mining. Countries share their results, and visitors from one station often drop in on another for dinner, which may be the only party within 500 kilometres.

text: A fjord (say "fee-ORD") is a long, narrow arm of the sea that winds far inland between steep mountain walls. Fjords were carved by [[@glaciers|glaciers]] during the ice ages. As the ice melted and the sea level rose, seawater flowed into the deep valleys the ice had left behind.

Norway's west coast is the most famous fjord coast on Earth. The word "fjord" itself is Norwegian. Its fjords can be more than a kilometre deep, with waterfalls pouring off cliffs hundreds of metres high and tiny farms clinging to ledges above the water. Fjords also exist in [[@world-greenland|Greenland]], Alaska, Canada, Chile and New Zealand, all places that were covered by thick ice.

st.prompt: Fjords are filled with water from the sea. So is the water in a fjord salty or fresh?

options.t: Salty, but often with a layer of fresher water on top from rivers and melting snow

st.reveal: A fjord is an arm of the sea, so it holds salt water. Rivers and waterfalls pour fresh water in, and because fresh water is lighter, it often floats on top in a thin layer. In some fjords the surface tastes only slightly salty.

myth: Fjords were carved by rivers.
Rivers usually made the first valleys, but glaciers turned them into fjords. Huge tongues of ice ground the valleys much deeper and wider, into a U shape, and the sea flooded in when the ice melted.
facts: a long, narrow, deep inlet of the sea carved by glaciers

sec.t:
During the last [[@ice-ages|ice age]], a sheet of ice up to about 3 kilometres thick covered Scandinavia. The ice flowed slowly towards the sea, squeezing into existing river valleys. As it moved, it dragged rocks frozen into its base, which scraped and ground the valley floor like giant sandpaper.

River valleys are usually V-shaped. Glaciers turned them into deep U-shapes with flat floors and steep sides. The ice dug deepest where it was thickest, far inland, so many fjords are deeper inside than at their mouths. Near the sea there is often a shallow underwater ridge called a sill.

When the ice melted about 10,000 years ago, the sea rushed in. The land, freed from the weight of the ice, is still rising slowly, by a few millimetres a year in some places.

{{story:glaciers}}

The Sognefjord is Norway's longest fjord, stretching about 205 kilometres inland from the coast north of Bergen. That is longer than the drive from Mumbai to Nashik. Its deepest point is about 1,300 metres below the surface.

One of its narrow side branches, the Nærøyfjord, is only about 250 metres wide in places. Together with the Geirangerfjord, famous for the Seven Sisters waterfalls, it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005. Because there are so many fjords and islands, Norway's coastline, if you followed every bend, would be about 100,000 kilometres long, enough to go around the Earth two and a half times.

For centuries, the easiest way to travel in western Norway was by boat. Steep mountains blocked roads, but fjords made water highways. The [[@vikings|Vikings]] built their longships in sheltered fjords and sailed out from them to trade and raid across Europe.

Today, car ferries still cross many fjords. Some of them, on routes such as the Sognefjord, run on batteries. Engineers have also drilled [[@extreme-longest-tunnels|long road tunnels]] through the mountains. The Lærdal Tunnel, opened in 2000, is about 24.5 kilometres long, the longest road tunnel in the world. Drivers pass through three large caves lit in blue and yellow, designed to keep them alert.

sec.h: Warm water in the far north
sec.t:
Norway reaches far north of the Arctic Circle, yet its fjords and harbours mostly stay free of ice in winter. The reason is the North Atlantic Current, a branch of the Gulf Stream, which carries warm water from the tropics up the coast. These [[@ocean-currents|ocean currents]] make Norway's coast much milder than places at the same latitude in Canada or Siberia.

In winter in the far north, the sun doesn't rise for weeks, but the [[@stargazing|dark skies]] are often lit by the green curtains of the [[@solar-wind|northern lights]]. In summer the opposite happens, and the midnight sun shines all night.

text: Almost every alphabet in use today, from English to Greek to Hebrew to Arabic, comes from one invention made about 3,800 years ago. People who spoke a Semitic language, related to today's Arabic and Hebrew, borrowed a few Egyptian [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] and used them in a new way. Instead of standing for whole words, each picture now stood for a single sound.
That idea was simple and powerful. Egyptian writing used hundreds of signs and took years to master. An alphabet needs only a few dozen, so far more people could learn to read and write.
India's main family of scripts has its own, debated story, which begins with a script called Brahmi.

st.prompt: The letter A started out as a small picture. A picture of what?
st.reveal: The early sign aleph meant ox and showed an ox's head with horns. Over centuries it tipped on its side and then stood on its point, becoming our A. Flip a capital A over and the horns reappear.

d.try: Invent your own alphabet the way the first letter-makers did. For each sound in your name, draw a tiny picture of something that starts with that sound, like a mango for "m" or a sun for "s". Write a short message in your picture-letters and give a friend the key to decode it.

sec.t:
The early alphabet worked by a clever rule: a picture stood for the first sound of its name. The sign for an ox, *aleph*, stood for the sound at the start of that word. A sign for a house, *bet*, stood for "b". A wavy line for water, *mem*, stood for "m".

Examples of this early writing have been found at Serabit el-Khadim, an ancient turquoise mine in the Sinai desert, and at Wadi el-Hol in Egypt. They are short, scratched lines, probably made by workers, miners or soldiers rather than by royal scribes. It's a nice thought. The alphabet may have been invented by ordinary people who found Egyptian writing far too complicated.

Around 800 BCE, the Greeks borrowed the Phoenician letters. Greek words were hard to read without vowels, so the Greeks took some Phoenician signs for sounds they didn't use and turned them into vowels. *Aleph* became *alpha*, the letter A. For the first time, an alphabet wrote down every consonant and every vowel.

The Greek alphabet passed to the Etruscans in Italy and then to the Romans, whose Latin alphabet is the one you are reading now. Letters flipped, turned and changed shape along the way. The ox head lay on its side and finally stood on its point, which is why a capital A turned upside down still shows two horns. The Romans' letters went on to spread across Europe and, much later, to the Americas.

In India, the oldest readable script is Brahmi, best known from the rock and pillar messages of Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] in the 3rd century BCE. Brahmi is the ancestor of most modern Indian scripts, including Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil and Telugu, and of many scripts across Southeast Asia.

Where Brahmi came from is debated. Many scholars think its makers were inspired by a Semitic script such as Aramaic, which was used in the [[@ancient-persia|Persian Empire]] next door. Others argue it developed within India. Either way, Brahmi organised its sounds in a very Indian way, grouping them by where they are made in the mouth. You can follow that story in [[@scripts-india|India's many scripts]].

India's oldest writing of all, the [[@indus-script|Indus script]], is older still. Nobody has managed to read it yet.

text: Top spellers don't memorise every word. They learn how words are built. English has borrowed words from Latin, Greek, French, German, Hindi, Japanese and hundreds of other languages, and each language brings its own spelling habits. A champion who hears an unfamiliar word asks for its meaning, its language of origin and an example sentence. Then they use what they know about roots and patterns to work it out.

That is why spellers at the Scripps National Spelling Bee in the USA are allowed to ask those questions on stage. Behind every winning word are years of practice, thousands of flashcards and a lot of patient parents and coaches.

st.prompt: In a spelling bee, a speller can ask for a word's language of origin. Why does that help?

The judges give an easier word if you ask
It tells you how many letters the word has

st.reveal: Words borrowed from Greek often use "ph" for the f sound, French words often end in "-eau", and Italian ones may double consonants. Knowing where a word came from narrows down the spelling, like a clue in a puzzle.

Look each one up in a dictionary to find its language of origin, and write down any pattern you notice, like "rh" or "ph" in Greek words. Then test a friend and give them the origin as a clue.
myth: Spelling bee champions just memorise the whole dictionary.

No one can memorise the hundreds of thousands of words in a big dictionary. Champions learn many lists, but mostly they learn roots, word origins and spelling patterns, so they can work out words they have never seen.

sec.t:
Say the word sounds like "fy-LOG-uh-nee" and comes from Greek. A good speller knows Greek words often use "ph" for f and "y" for a short i. They might know the root *phylo*, meaning a tribe or group, as in "phylum". So they try *phylogeny*, and they are right.

Champions study [[@latin-roots|Latin roots]] like *aqua*, water, and *scribe*, write. They learn that French words often hide silent letters, like the "t" in "ballet", and that Dutch words can use "oo" and "aa". English spelling looks chaotic, but much of it makes sense once you know where a word came from.

In 2019, eight spellers kept getting every word right deep into the night. The organisers had planned only so many rounds and felt the words left in their list wouldn't challenge them. So all eight were named co-champions, nicknamed the Octochamps. Since then, the bee has added tie-breaking spell-offs.

The bee has also added vocabulary questions, where spellers choose a word's meaning, so knowing what words mean now matters as much as spelling them.

In 1985, Balu Natarajan, from Illinois, became the first Indian-American to win. Since 1999, children of Indian heritage have won most of the titles, including the 2025 champion, Faizan Zaki from Texas.

People suggest several reasons. Many [[@indian-diaspora|Indian-American families]] put strong value on study and competitions. A network of smaller bees, run by community groups, lets children practise for years. Older siblings coach younger ones. And success inspires others: each champion makes the next generation believe they can win too.

India has its own spelling bees too, in English and in Indian languages. Some schools run them in Hindi, where the spelling of a word is usually much closer to its sound than in English.

English spelling is hard partly because English borrows so freely, including from India. Words like "bungalow", "shampoo", "jungle" and "pyjamas" all came from Indian languages. To spell those at a bee, it helps to know their history, which is one more reason the stories behind [[@words-borrowed|borrowed words]] are worth learning. And the reason English sticks to messy old spellings at all lies in its history in [[@dictionaries|dictionaries]], which froze many of them hundreds of years ago.
